read.sections.0.text.note: Timor-Leste and Indonesia: politically sensitive. "Indonesia controlled it" is อินโดนีเซียเข้าควบคุม, kept neutral as in the English. Second pass: "independence was restored" is เอกราช...ฟื้นคืนมา across the whole course (glossary word ฟื้นคืน, which the checker needs in both texts; the timeline event, the picture label, visual.alt, and now also the section check war-and-independence, which said ได้เอกราชคืน). The course text never had the phrase. A native speaker may still prefer ได้เอกราชคืน; if so, the glossary word must change with it.
read.sections.0.text.source: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote run by the United Nations. Most voted to begin a move towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. A transition followed. A United Nations team ran the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. It had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate on one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.
read.sections.0.text.back: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia took control of it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote organised by the United Nations. Most voted to begin moving towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition. A United Nations team looked after running the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. It had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate on one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition. A United Nations team helped run the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate in one day. But good schools for every child take much longer.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Timor-Leste has another name, East Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. Later Indonesia took control. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave home. Then came a transition. A United Nations team helped look after the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate on one day, but good schools for every child take much longer.

read.sections.1.text.note: Tetum written ภาษาเตตุม (check spelling). UNESCO written ยูเนสโก in Thai prose to match the course text; kept Latin in source titles.
read.sections.1.text.source: Rebuilding schools began during the transition, not after it. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children who had been in primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped restart their schools. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher called Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events. It is not a diary written by a child in 1999.
read.sections.1.text.back: Rebuilding schools began during the transition, not after it. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children who had been in primary school had come back. Many schools were repaired; many got new roofs. In some areas, teachers, parents and communities helped open schools again. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher named Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events; it is not a diary written by a child in 1999.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Work on schools started during the transition. It did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report said most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people fixed buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: School repairs began in the transition. They did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children were back in school. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people repaired buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and language came later.

read.sections.2.text.source: The Government of Timor-Leste lists Tetum and Portuguese as the official languages. People also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the United Nations' agency for children, says the country has rebuilt its schools since 2002, and more children now go to school. It also names problems: old buildings, many languages, and fewer school facilities in country areas. UNICEF works with the government on school repairs, teaching and schools where students and parents take part. The photo shows one school in 2024. It cannot tell us if students there have books or trained teachers. It cannot show if they have access to lessons in a language they know.
read.sections.2.text.back: The government of Timor-Leste names Tetum and Portuguese as official languages. People also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the United Nations agency for children, says the country has rebuilt schools since 2002 and more children now go to school. UNICEF also names problems: old buildings, many languages, and fewer school facilities in rural areas. UNICEF works with the government on repairing schools, teaching, and schools where students and parents take part. The photo shows one school in 2024. It cannot tell us whether the students there have books or trained teachers, and cannot show whether they have access to lessons in a language they know.

watch.summary.source: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. It visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountains of Timor-Leste. After the vote in 1999, many people left their homes. The school was left with no roof, desks or chairs. When people came back, local school leaders asked teachers to return. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education says the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, fix schools and train teachers. Now the school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Students and parents take part in school life.
watch.summary.back: This UNICEF report, made in 2011, visits a primary school in Laclubar (Laclubar), a mountain town in Timor-Leste. After the 1999 vote, many people left their homes. The school was left without a roof, desks or chairs. When people came back, the local school leader asked teachers to come back and teach. Parents gave chairs, desks and other things the school needed. The Minister of Education says the country had to restart schools from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, repair schools and train teachers. Now the school uses child-friendly teaching. Students and parents take part in the life of the school.

Some learners have lived through violence or had to leave their homes: never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, violence or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and let anyone step out of a discussion without a reason. sensitiveNotes.0.back: The 1999 vote was followed by severe violence and the displacement of many people. The lesson states this directly in one sentence; don't add detail or images. Some learners have experienced violence or had to leave home. Do not ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, violence or displacement, or about home country, religion or ethnicity, and let anyone leave the discussion without giving a reason. educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners choose two priorities for rebuilding education, give a source-based reason for each, and name a trade-off. Evidence move: ask what a school needs besides walls. A sound answer gives two priorities supported by the UN report, the IIEP study or UNICEF, and a reasonable trade-off. Misconceptions to address: "independence instantly solved education", "education work only started after 2002", and "all learners speak both official languages".

educatorNotes.1.source: Languages: the Government of Timor-Leste lists Portuguese and Tetum (Tétum, the national language) as official, English and Indonesian as working languages, and about 15 other local languages. Talk about this without deficit framing: many languages are a strength and a planning question, not a problem in children. Source caveats: UNICEF's page gives percentages with no date, so the lesson does not use them as current rates. The IIEP abstract dates the consultation to September 1999 (the vote was on 30 August; the result came in September). The UN news item shows only "23 March"; its address and content (UNTAET, the earlier international force) place it in 2000.
